title: The Librarian on the Hill
subtitle: A slow sleep story for tonight
about: An invented story about a librarian who closes a quiet hilltop library on an autumn evening and goes to sleep. Not a true story.
text:
Welcome. This story is invented, and it is meant to be heard slowly. There is nothing to remember, and nothing to work out. If you fall asleep before the end, that is exactly right, and the story will carry on gently without you.

Let your body grow heavy against the bed. Let your shoulders drop, and your hands open. Breathe in slowly through your nose, and breathe out through your mouth, like a long, quiet sigh. Once more. In, and out. Good.

Now picture a small library on the top of a green hill, on an evening in the middle of autumn. The hill is covered in old oak trees, and their leaves have turned the colour of honey and copper. A few of them drift down, one at a time, and settle on the path without a sound.

The library is a long, low building made of grey stone, with a roof of dark slate and a round window above the door. The windows glow a soft amber, because someone has already lit the lamps. A thin thread of smoke rises from the chimney, and leans a little in the wind, and fades.

The librarian is called Ines Marlowe. She is a slight, quiet woman of sixty-three, with silver hair pinned up under a pencil, round glasses on a cord, and a long green cardigan with deep pockets. In one pocket she keeps a ball of string. In the other, a small, worn notebook.

Ines has looked after this library for twenty-six years. It is a calm place, and few people come, only a handful each week, and they come to read, not to talk. On most evenings, once the last visitor has gone, she locks the front door and begins the slow work of closing the day.

She starts at the entrance, and walks along the main aisle. The floor is made of wide oak boards, polished by many feet, and they give a faint, friendly creak with every step. Ines walks slowly. She has never hurried in this building, and the building has never asked her to.

On either side stand the shelves, tall and dark, reaching almost to the ceiling. They are filled with books of every size, thin ones and thick ones, with spines of green and brown and faded red. The air smells of paper, and leather, and a little of woodsmoke, and of the rain that fell this morning.

At the first shelf she stops, and runs her fingers along the spines, lightly, as one might stroke the back of a sleeping animal. She straightens a book that leans, and pushes another a little deeper, until every spine lines up in a soft, even row.

At the end of the aisle stands the old card catalogue, a wide wooden cabinet with a hundred small drawers. Each drawer has a brass handle shaped like a tiny shell, and a little label written long ago in a careful hand. Ines slides one open, and it glides out with a soft, papery whisper, full of neat cream cards, each one standing upright like a row of sleeping birds.

She does not look for anything in particular. She simply lets her fingers walk across the tops of the cards, and feels the slight bump of each one. A, and B, and C. The names of authors, and the names of places, and the names of things that no one has asked about for years, all kept safe, all waiting, in the cool dark of the drawer.

There is a ladder on wheels, and she rolls it along the rail to the next section. It glides with a low, wooden rumble. She climbs three steps, and takes down a book with a faded blue cover, and blows a little dust from the top edge, and the dust floats in the lamplight like pale gold.

This is her evening habit. She does not read the books, only checks that each one is where it belongs. She finds this very restful. There is a quiet pleasure in order, in a world where everything has a place, and the place is known, and nothing is lost.

A grandfather clock stands near the reading tables, tall and thin, with a brass face. Its ticking is slow and deep, like the footsteps of someone walking through a very large house. Beneath the clock, a long table holds a row of green lamps, each one casting a small, warm circle on the wood.

Ines walks to the tables, and tidies the chairs, pushing each one in with a gentle nudge. She gathers a few forgotten pencils, and a folded scrap of paper, and a single grey glove, and puts them into the little basket for lost things that sits beside the clock.

The basket is nearly always full of small treasures. Sometimes the owners come back for them, and sometimes they do not. In the spring she empties it, and gives the gloves to the village, and the pencils to the school, and everything finds a home again, in its own time.

On the way, she passes the map room, a small alcove with a slanted table and a lamp on a swinging arm. The maps are rolled in long cardboard tubes, and stacked in a rack like a bundle of quiet flutes. One is unrolled, held flat with four smooth stones. It shows a river winding through a green valley, with every bend drawn by hand.

Ines looks at it for a moment, and follows the river with her eyes, from the hills down to the sea. The river is slow, and wide, and unhurried. It passes small villages, and bridges, and fields with tiny trees, and it never once seems to worry about where it is going. She rolls the map up gently, and slides it into its tube.

Now she goes to the window at the far end, where a deep stone sill holds a row of potted plants. There is a small fern, and a trailing ivy, and a pot of violets that bloom, against all the rules, in the middle of autumn. She waters each one from a copper can.

The water trickles into the soil with a soft, dark sound. The leaves of the fern tremble, and settle. Ines lets a few drops fall on the violets, and she says, very quietly, there you are. She has said it to the violets every evening for years.

Outside, the wind moves through the oaks, and the leaves whisper against each other like pages being turned. Far below the hill, in the valley, a few lights glimmer in the village, small and yellow, and a curl of mist lies along the river, white and still.

When the watering is done, she goes to the little room behind the front desk, where the kettle waits on a small iron stove. She fills it, and lights the stove, and while it warms, she takes down a blue cup, and a tin of dried apple and cinnamon tea.

The kettle begins to sing, softly at first, then a little louder. Ines pours the water over the tea, and the smell rises, sweet and warm, like an orchard in the sun. She carries the cup in both hands, back out into the long room, and sets it on the nearest table.

Before she sits, she stops at the tall clock, and opens its glass door with a small brass key. Inside, the pendulum swings slowly, left and right, left and right, a golden pause between each stroke. She lifts the winding crank, and turns it eleven times, and each turn gives a soft, ratcheting click, like a very small and patient cricket.

When the clock is wound, she closes the door, and listens. The ticking sounds a little brighter, and a little surer, as though it had taken a deep breath. Ines smiles. She has wound this clock every evening for twenty-six years, and every evening it seems to thank her, in its own steady way.

There is an armchair beside the stove in the corner, deep and worn, with a patchwork blanket folded over its arm. Ines sits down in it, and tucks the blanket over her knees, and holds the warm cup against her chest. Her shoulders sink, and her breath grows slow.

She does not take a book. Tonight she simply sits and listens. The clock ticks, the stove crackles, and the wind sighs in the chimney. There is a particular kind of peace in a room full of books, as though all the stories were sleeping, and breathing very softly together.

The stove glows through its little mica window, a small orange eye, calm and steady. Every few minutes a log settles with a soft, warm thud, and a handful of sparks drifts up and fades. Ines watches them rise, and her mind grows quiet, and wide, and still, like a lake without a breeze.

A grey cat steps out from between two shelves. Her name is Quill, and she lives here, as much as she lives anywhere. She stretches her front paws, and yawns, and walks across the floorboards without a sound, and jumps up lightly onto the arm of the chair.

Ines strokes her, once, along the back. Quill turns around twice, and settles in her lap, and begins to purr, a low, soft, steady engine. The warmth of her small body spreads across Ines's knees, and the two of them sit together in the lamplight, content and quiet.

Beyond the round window, the sky is deepening. The last orange light has slipped behind the hills, and a pale blue is rising, and then a darker blue, and then, one by one, the stars come out. The first is bright and low. Then another, and another, until the whole window is dusted with silver.

Outside, a light rain begins. It is very fine, hardly more than a mist, and it makes a faint, soft hush against the glass of the round window. Drops gather on the panes, and run slowly down, and join together, and leave thin, silver trails. The oak leaves darken, and glisten, and their whispering deepens into something rounder and calmer.

Ines listens to the rain, and does not mind it. The library is warm and dry, and the rain only makes the room feel safer, like a blanket tucked in at the edges. She lets her head rest against the back of the chair, and her eyes half close, and the rain sings its small, endless song.

The tea grows cool in the cup. Ines finishes it in small sips, and sets it down. The tiredness she feels is a gentle kind, the kind that comes after an ordinary day done well, and it settles in her limbs like warm sand, heavy and soft and welcome.

At last she gets up, lifting the cat carefully and setting her on the cushion of the chair. Quill curls into a ring and goes on purring. Ines folds the blanket, and goes around the room, turning down each lamp, one by one, until only a single small light is left.

The shelves slip into shadow. The books grow dim and quiet, rows and rows of them, dark shapes against the walls, holding their stories close. The clock ticks on. The stove ticks softly as it cools. And the whole long room seems to settle, like a ship coming to rest in a harbour.

Ines climbs a narrow wooden stair at the back of the library, to the small room where she sleeps. It has a sloping ceiling, and a round window, and a narrow bed under a patchwork quilt. A lamp burns on the table, and a glass of water stands beside it.

On the little table by the bed lies a single book, with a ribbon marking the page. It is a gentle book about a garden, and she has been reading it for many weeks, a page or two each night, never in a hurry. Tonight she does not open it. She rests her hand on the cover for a moment, and feels the soft, worn cloth.

Beside the book sits a small ceramic dish, holding a smooth grey pebble that she found long ago by the river. She picks it up, and turns it over in her palm. It is cool, and heavy, and perfectly round. She puts it back in the dish, and the little click it makes is the last sound she makes before the quiet.

She sits on the edge of the bed, and takes off her glasses, and rubs the bridge of her nose. She lets her cardigan slide from her shoulders, and hangs it on a hook. She unpins her hair, and it falls, silver and soft, over her shoulders, and she sighs.

She lies down, and draws the quilt up to her chin. The pillow is cool, and then warm. Through the round window she can see a single star, steady and small, hanging above the hill. She watches it for a while, and her eyelids grow heavy, as though they were made of velvet.

Below her, the library is breathing. The old boards creak and settle as the night air cools them. The wind brushes the roof slates, and the oak leaves whisper, and somewhere downstairs the cat turns over in her sleep, and the clock goes on counting out the quiet hours, one by one.

Ines thinks of the books, all in their places. She thinks of the violets, and the glow of the stove, and the cup she left on the table, which she will wash tomorrow. She thinks of nothing at all, and the thinking slowly melts away, like frost in the early sun.

Her breathing slows, and lengthens. Her hands lie open on the quilt. There is nothing left to tidy, or to carry, or to check. There is only the soft, deep dark behind her eyes, and the sound of her own breath, rising and falling, like a tide on a gentle shore.

And somewhere in the middle of that rhythm, Ines falls asleep. Her face is calm. The quilt rises and falls with her breath. The star in the window goes on shining, and the hill goes on holding the library, and the library goes on holding the quiet.

Now it is your turn to do just the same. Let your breath find its own pace. Let your arms and legs grow heavy, as if the bed were holding every part of you. Let your jaw rest, and your brow soften, and your thoughts drift away like leaves on a slow river.

Imagine, if you like, that you are lying in a small room under a sloping ceiling, with the soft sound of the wind in the oak trees outside. Each breath is a slow wave. Each wave carries a little more of the day away, and leaves behind a little more calm.

There is nothing left to do. The lamps are low, and the shelves are quiet, and the whole hill is resting under the stars. You are warm, and you are safe, and the whole of the long autumn night is yours to rest in.

You can rest now.

Goodnight.
